questions.q: Why does the workflow insist on reproducing the actual query with real parameter values and representative data volume?
options: A query can behave completely differently at production scale or with a specific parameter value than it does on a small test table, so testing under different conditions can hide the real problem
SQL Server only allows execution plans to be captured against production data
Reproducing the exact conditions is optional and mainly saves time
Test tables always produce identical plans to production tables
questions.explain: Data volume and specific parameter values can change which plan the optimizer picks entirely, so an unrepresentative reproduction can point you at the wrong fix or hide the real one.

questions.q: Per the workflow, what does "isolate" mean?
options: Narrowing a multi-part problem down to the specific operator, wait type, or resource actually driving the cost, rather than tuning everything at once
Running the query on an isolated server with no other users connected
Disabling all indexes before testing a query
Isolating the transaction using SERIALIZABLE isolation level
questions.explain: A query with many joins might have just one expensive join; isolating means finding that one specific driver instead of broadly attacking everything.

questions.q: Why does the workflow require making exactly one change at a time?
options: Bundling multiple changes into one deployment means you can't tell which change caused an observed improvement, or whether one change is masking a regression from another
SQL Server technically only allows one schema change per transaction
Multiple changes always cancel each other out
It's a licensing restriction in SQL Server Standard Edition
questions.explain: If an index, a rewrite, and a MAXDOP hint all ship together and performance improves, you have no way to know which one actually mattered.

questions.q: What is a properly formed hypothesis, per this lesson's example?
options: "This Key Lookup is expensive because there's no covering index for these columns" — a specific, falsifiable guess
"Indexes might help"
"The server just needs more RAM"
"It's probably a bug in SQL Server itself"
questions.explain: A good hypothesis names a specific operator and a specific reason, so a single targeted change can confirm or disprove it.

questions.q: Why does the workflow end with a documentation step?
options: So the problem, the change made, and the measured before/after are on record for when the same symptom recurs or someone asks whether it was already fixed
Documentation is required by SQL Server licensing terms
It has no real purpose beyond bureaucratic compliance
It replaces the need to verify the change actually worked
questions.explain: Recording what was diagnosed, changed, and measured gives future-you or another DBA a reference for recurring or related issues.
